title: Aadhaar for NRIs and OCI Holders: Current Rules and UIDAI’s Global Expansion Plan
excerpt: As UIDAI works to take Aadhaar international, here are the rules that apply today: NRIs with Indian passports can apply on arrival but must visit India in person; OCI holders face a 182-day stay requirement.
body:
• NRIs holding valid Indian passports are exempt from the 182-day residency rule and can apply for Aadhaar immediately on arrival in India — but must still visit an enrolment centre in person for biometrics.
  • OCI cardholders face stricter rules: they are treated as resident foreign nationals and must have lived in India for at least 182 days in the 12 months before applying, enrolling in person with their OCI card, foreign passport, and Indian address proof.
  • UIDAI CEO Saurabh Vijay told Global Fintech Fest 2026 that proof-of-concept work is underway to make Aadhaar “international,” with the legal framework and OCI-specific policies in development.
  • UIDAI is deploying AI extensively for fraud detection, handles 10 crore authentications a day, and is building infrastructure for 25–30 crore daily authentications.

The Unique Identification Authority of India is working to take Aadhaar global — but for the diaspora, the question that matters right now is simpler: what are the enrolment rules today? Under current regulations, the answer splits sharply between NRIs and OCI cardholders, and the gap between the two is wide.

Current rules for NRIs

For non-resident Indians holding a valid Indian passport, the application process is straightforward. The standard 182-day residency requirement is waived, allowing NRIs to apply immediately upon arrival in India. But there is no online alternative: applicants must still physically visit an authorized Aadhaar Enrolment Centre in India to complete biometric verification.

Current rules for OCI cardholders

Overseas Citizens of India face a stricter regime. OCI cardholders are currently classified alongside resident foreign nationals for Aadhaar purposes, and must physically reside in India for at least 182 days within the 12 months immediately preceding their application date. Once eligible, they must submit their valid OCI card and foreign passport, along with applicable proof of an Indian address, during their in-person enrolment.

The global plan

The rules explain why UIDAI’s global push matters. CEO Saurabh Vijay said at the Global Fintech Fest 2026 in Mumbai that his ambition is to make Aadhaar infrastructure best in class to facilitate the platform’s global expansion. “I think for Aadhaar, the focus now is on making Aadhaar international. We really want to work on the interoperability part of it — how to make it more possible. So already some PoCs (proof of concept) are happening,” he said during a fireside chat on digital identity as public infrastructure.

“Our legal framework is also going in that direction to make Aadhaar international. We are working on policies to make it available for overseas citizens of India (OCIs) so that it brings in more investment,” Vijay added. He did not specify which countries or systems are involved in the proof-of-concept work — one PoC is reported to be in the Middle East — or provide a timeline for an international interoperability system.

Separately, India’s IFSCA is piloting Aadhaar face authentication in the UAE to onboard NRIs digitally, with the pilot expected to extend to the U.S. and two more countries — an early sign of what cross-border Aadhaar authentication could look like.

AI, fraud, and scale

At the same event, UIDAI Chairman Neelkanth Mishra said the authority is deploying artificial intelligence extensively to detect and counter fraud, describing an ongoing “cat-and-mouse game” with fraudsters. “Fraudsters keep getting smarter, but we are also getting smarter,” he said, noting that UIDAI had liveness tests on face and thumbprints long before AI became a buzzword.

“Fraudsters keep getting smarter, but we are also getting smarter. UIDAI is using AI extensively for fraud detection.”

— Neelkanth Mishra, Chairman, UIDAI

Mishra said daily Aadhaar authentications had risen “dramatically” from about seven crore when he first wrote UIDAI’s annual report to 10 crore now, and that the authority is preparing its infrastructure to handle 25–30 crore authentications a day. Vijay also flagged “Aadhaar Light,” a planned product for small merchants, with guidelines expected soon, and said the National Payments Corporation of India launched three products at the event, some of which may go international.

What it means for the diaspora

For the 36-million-strong Indian diaspora, the current rules remain the binding reality: an NRI trip to India is still required for enrolment, and OCI holders face the steep 182-day stay condition that has long been a grievance. The policy work Vijay described — particularly OCI-specific liberalization — is the development that could change that, by removing the stay requirement that keeps most overseas citizens of India out of the system.

What to watch

Three things will signal whether the global plan is moving from talk to action: the legal framework changes UIDAI says are in the works, the promised OCI policy liberalization, and the results of the international interoperability PoCs. Until those land, the in-person enrolment requirement stands — and the trip to India remains part of getting an Aadhaar.
